subject: Is your app's public code giving away your secret keys?
title: Keep secret API keys out of your frontend code
body: When you build an app with an AI tool, it is easy to end up with secret keys in the code that runs in the browser. Anything in your site's public JavaScript can be read by any visitor, including payment keys, AI provider keys and database admin keys.

Some keys are meant to be public. A Supabase anon key is normal, for example, but it is only safe if Row Level Security is turned on for every table. A Supabase service_role key is different: it bypasses all of your database rules and should never reach the browser.

The fix is to move secret keys into server-side environment variables, such as an Edge Function or API route, and have the browser call that. If a key has already been exposed, revoke it and create a new one.

subject: Can Google actually read your app's pages?
title: Check what Google sees when it opens your app
body: Many apps built with AI tools are single-page apps: the server sends a nearly empty HTML file, and JavaScript fills in the content in the browser. Google can run JavaScript, but rendering can be delayed, and pages that all share one generic title and description are hard to tell apart in search results.

A quick check: open your site, right-click and choose View Page Source. If your page title, description and main text are missing from that raw HTML, search engines and link previews have less to work with.

To fix it, give each page its own title and meta description, add a sitemap.xml, and make sure robots.txt is not blocking pages you want found. For your most important pages, consider pre-rendering or server-side rendering.

subject: Is your site sending the security headers browsers look for?
title: Add basic security headers to your app
body: Security headers are short instructions your server sends with every page. They tell the browser how to protect your visitors, and apps built with AI tools often go live without them, because many hosting setups do not add them by default.

Four worth having: Strict-Transport-Security keeps visitors on HTTPS, X-Content-Type-Options stops browsers from guessing file types, X-Frame-Options or a frame-ancestors rule stops other sites from loading yours in a hidden frame, and a Content-Security-Policy limits which scripts can run.

Most hosts let you add them in one config file, such as vercel.json, a Netlify _headers file, or your server's middleware. Start the Content-Security-Policy in report-only mode so you can see what it would block before it breaks anything.

subject: Can anyone with your Supabase key read your users' data?
title: Turn on Row Level Security for every Supabase table
body: If your app uses Supabase, its public anon key is built into your frontend code by design. That is only safe when Row Level Security (RLS) is turned on for every table, because RLS is what stops someone holding that key from reading or changing other people's data.
In the Supabase dashboard, check each table in your public schema. Any table without RLS enabled can be queried directly by anyone who has the key, without going through your app at all.

Turning RLS on with no policies blocks all access, so add policies next, such as letting signed-in users read and update only rows where user_id matches auth.uid(). Then test it: sign in as a second user and confirm you cannot see the first user's data.

subject: Can anyone download your app's .env file?
title: Make sure your .env and .git files are not publicly reachable
body: Apps built with AI tools often start in a folder that holds more than the app itself: a .env file with keys and passwords, a .git folder with your full code history, and sometimes backup or database export files. If that whole folder is uploaded to your host, those files can end up downloadable by anyone who guesses the address.
A quick check: in a private browser window, open your-site.com/.env and your-site.com/.git/config. You should get a 404 or your normal not-found page, not file contents.

To fix it, deploy only your build output folder (often dist or build), keep .env in .gitignore, and set secrets in your host's environment variable settings instead. If a file was ever reachable, treat every key in it as exposed: revoke it and create a new one.
